stimulus.text: Paraphrase: More than a million Black Americans served in the armed forces during World War II, most of them in segregated units. The best-known Black combat units were the Tuskegee Airmen, the first Black military pilots, who flew escort missions over Europe, and the 761st Tank Battalion. Japanese American soldiers of the 442nd Regimental Combat Team fought in Italy and France while many of their families were held in relocation camps at home. Navajo Marines in the Pacific sent radio messages in a code built on the Navajo language that Japanese code-breakers never broke. Black leaders called the fight the 'Double V': victory over fascism abroad and victory over racism at home.
stimulus.source_note: Original secondary summary drawn from Barron's Chapter 9 (Tuskegee Airmen; 761st Tank Battalion; Double V; 1.2 million Black Americans served; desegregation in 1948) and standard accounts of the 442nd Regimental Combat Team and the Navajo code talkers, verified against public sources. The books do not name the 442nd or the code talkers; both are named in the topic scope.

source: original; stimulus drawn from book-grounded figures and paraphrases (see source_note)
stem: According to the passage, who were the Tuskegee Airmen?

options.text: Japanese American soldiers who fought in Italy and France
options.misconception: That describes the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, not the Tuskegee Airmen.

options.text: Navajo Marines who sent coded radio messages in the Pacific
options.misconception: That describes the Navajo code talkers, not the Tuskegee Airmen.

options.text: White bomber pilots who flew bombing missions over Japan
options.misconception: The Tuskegee Airmen were Black fighter pilots who escorted bombers over Europe.

options.text: The first Black military pilots, who flew escort missions over Europe

rationales.A: The 442nd was Japanese American and fought in Italy and France.
rationales.B: The Navajo code talkers sent coded messages in the Pacific.
rationales.C: The Tuskegee Airmen were Black pilots, not white bomber pilots.
rationales.D: The passage calls them the first Black military pilots, flying escort over Europe.
rationales.general:
1. The passage names the Tuskegee Airmen as the first Black military pilots.
2. It says they flew escort missions over Europe.
3. Background from the books: they served in segregated units, like most Black troops in the war.
4. Their record helped make the case for desegregating the armed forces in 1948.
Remember: a unit's name often tells its story, so match each unit to its own description.
